name: Tara Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise the site crews for a company that builds timber-frame houses in a factory and then puts them together on site. So the wall panels arrive on a lorry at seven, already insulated, windows in, and my crew of eight lifts them into place with the crane and fixes them. On a good day we close in a whole house, walls and roof, in two days. Then I'm on the laptop at lunch checking tomorrow's delivery against the drawings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's clever. I spent twenty-five years building houses stick by stick in the rain, and this is faster, drier and less wasteful, and the houses are warmer. What wears me down is the lorries being late, and the crane hire costing a fortune by the hour while we wait. And I'm fifty-eight, so the ladders are less fun than they were.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every single day. My crew speaks five languages between them, so I write the morning safety talk and get the AI to put it into each language, then I check with someone who speaks it. I use it to sort out delivery schedules and to check a drawing for clashes. My husband David, he's a retired paramedic, says I talk to it more than I talk to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: that's a bit of a letdown. At work I'd say we keep using what works, the translations and the scheduling, and stop pretending it'll build the houses. Online I'd probably post something like, turns out the hard part of building is still the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. I've got about four years left, maybe five, a good salary, savings, and David's pension. I'd actually be a little disappointed, because I'd hoped it would make the job safer and easier for the people coming after me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am, keep using the tools I already use. I'd probably push the company to try the newer scheduling software, since cranes standing idle cost us so much. Other than that, I'd keep saving and plan to stop at about sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a film that ends before the good bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hoped it would make the job safer. What did you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pictured a machine doing the worst jobs, like fixing roof sheets in a high wind. Last winter one of my lads, Dariusz, slipped on a wet panel, luckily he was clipped on. I'd love a robot to do that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in this picture a relief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Owen tests software for a bank, and he'd be safe in this one. So yes, if I'm honest, that part's a relief. I'd still be a bit disappointed, but I'd sleep fine.

S0.say: It's a letdown: keep the tools that work and stop pretending AI will build the houses. Online she'd post that the hard part of building is still the building.
S0.think: Her last four or five years stay the same, with a good salary, savings and her husband's pension. She'd be disappointed because she'd hoped AI would make the job safer for younger workers.
S0.do: Keeps working with the tools she already uses and pushes the company to try newer scheduling software to cut idle crane time. Keeps saving and plans to stop around sixty-two.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, disappointed more than relieved.
S0.quote: I'd probably post something like, turns out the hard part of building is still the building.
S0.fieldNote: Tara is the rare worker who's disappointed that AI stays small. Her hopes for it are about safety, illustrated by a crew member slipping on a wet panel. She admits relief for her son's job underneath the disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, about time, but share it out. At work I'd be the one showing people how to use the tools, and I'd say to management that if the factory gets faster, the crew should see it in their pay, not just the shareholders. I'd post about it, I'm one of those annoying people who posts about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good. Prefab is already halfway to automation, the factory has robot nailing lines, so I've seen this coming. My job turns into coordinating machines and people, which I'm good at, and I'd want to do it before I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd volunteer for any pilot the company runs, robot fixing, drones for roof checks, whatever. I'd do an online course on it in the evenings, I've already started one on drone surveying. And I'd sit with the union rep and work out a fair deal for anyone whose job shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the first day on a new kind of job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be the one showing people the tools. Who on your crew would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, probably. He's sixty-one, brilliant with a nail gun, and he still writes his hours on a cigarette packet. I'd sit with him on his breaks, not in a classroom, because that's where he'd learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company didn't share the gains with the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd make noise. I'm not shy, and I'm in the union, I'd get the rep involved and push for a productivity bonus. I'd stay and fight before I'd walk, because it's not the machines' fault.

S1.say: Good, about time, but share it out. She'd show people the tools and tell management the crew should see faster factories in their pay, not just shareholders.
S1.think: Mostly good for her: prefab is already halfway automated and her job would turn into coordinating machines and people, which suits her.
S1.do: Volunteers for every company pilot, from robot fixing to roof-check drones, and keeps up an evening course in drone surveying. Works with the union rep on a fair deal for anyone whose job shrinks.
S1.quote: He's sixty-one, brilliant with a nail gun, and he still writes his hours on a cigarette packet.
S1.fieldNote: Tara mixes early-adopter enthusiasm with a firm progressive line on sharing gains. She plans to bring a resistant older colleague along by teaching him on breaks. She'd fight inside the company rather than leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one moves much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to do it fairly. At work I'd say we need to slow the rollout until there's a plan for the crews. Online I'd back the calls for a pause and for some kind of basic income, because otherwise you'll have millions of people with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, money-wise, it's fine. I'd be sixty, we've got enough, I could stop. But Owen's job at the bank would be gone overnight, and my crew, most of them in their thirties with kids, would be competing with machines. That's what gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd talk to the company about leading the robot rollout on site, because if it's coming, I'd rather the person running it is someone who cares about the crew. I'd press them for a written promise on redeployment. And I'd be on the phone to the local MP, and I'd join whatever campaign the union started for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, honestly. I'm excited about the tools, but two years isn't enough for people to land on their feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be running the rollout. Doesn't that put you on the other side from your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and I've thought about it. I'd rather be inside the tent arguing than outside it watching. If they're going to use robots anyway, I want to be the one saying, keep Pete, keep Dariusz, retrain them to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's welcome to come and work with me, actually, he's good with computers and the robots will need people to set them up. He'd laugh, because he hates getting his shoes muddy. But I'd mean it.

S2.say: This is too fast to do fairly, so slow the rollout until there's a plan for the crews. She'd back calls for a pause and for a basic income.
S2.think: She'd be sixty and financially fine. What gets her is her son's bank job vanishing and her crew, mostly thirties with kids, competing with machines.
S2.do: Asks to lead the robot rollout on site so someone who cares about the crew runs it, and presses for a written redeployment promise. Calls the local MP and joins the union's campaign for income support.
S2.feel: Uneasy: excited about the tools but sure two years is too short for people to land.
S2.quote: I'd rather be inside the tent arguing than outside it watching.
S2.fieldNote: Tara takes the gap between her enthusiasm and her crew's risk head on. She chooses to lead the rollout rather than resist it, and is aware of the tension. Even in the fastest case she stays uneasy rather than anxious, because her money and skills feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable if we start today. At work I'd push for a training programme for every crew member, paid, during work hours. I'd write about it online, probably long posts nobody reads to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's the best version, really. I'd be sixty-three, and I could spend my last years setting up how robots and people work together on our sites. That's something I'd be proud to leave behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to make me a training lead for the robot crews, part time, while I still supervise. I'd finish the drone course and do another on robot safety. And I'd put a bit of our savings into a small fund the union is setting up to help retrain workers in our area, maybe five thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit purposeful. Like having a last big project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five thousand of your own savings is a lot. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've done well out of this trade, and the people who taught me didn't. My first foreman, Norm, retired with a bad back and nothing much else. If I can help someone avoid that, it's worth more than another holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy shares in the robot companies, which I know some of my friends would. It feels a bit like betting against my crew. Maybe that's daft, but it's how I feel.

S3.say: Five years is tight but workable if we start today. She'd push for paid training for every crew member during work hours.
S3.think: This is the best version for her: at sixty-three she could spend her last working years shaping how robots and people work together on site.
S3.do: Asks to become a part-time training lead for robot crews and does a robot safety course after finishing drone surveying. Puts about five thousand of her savings into a union retraining fund.
S3.feel: Calm and purposeful, like taking on a last big project.
S3.quote: My first foreman, Norm, retired with a bad back and nothing much else.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Tara's career end into a mission. She spends her own money on a union retraining fund, motivated by a debt to her first foreman. Refusing to buy robot shares shows her loyalty to the crew runs deeper than her love of the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make it good for everyone, so no excuses. I'd keep pushing for a shorter working week and for the gains to be shared. I'd probably say it at the union branch as a retired member by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's easy. I'd be sixty-eight and retired, probably teaching a course at the college on how to run a robot crew, if they'd have me. My kids would have ten years to adjust, which is plenty for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to about sixty-two, using every new tool as it comes. After retiring, I'd offer to teach at the college part time. I'd help Owen and Mei plan, Mei runs a café and might want to look at what machines could do in her kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit envious of the young ones, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Envious? Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'll get to do this job without wrecking their bodies. I've got a shoulder that clicks every time I lift my arm above my head. If a robot means some twenty-year-old never gets that click, I'm jealous and glad at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your crew's lives look like in 2036, in the best case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the best case, they work three or four days, they run the machines, and they're paid like skilled people, because they are. In the worst case, they're gone and a company in some other city collects the money. Which one we get depends on what we fight for now.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to make it good for everyone, so no excuses. She'd keep pushing for a shorter week and shared gains, as a retired union member.
S4.think: She'll be sixty-eight and retired, maybe teaching how to run robot crews, and her children have ten years to adjust.
S4.do: Works to about sixty-two using every new tool, then offers to teach part time at the college. Helps her son and her daughter, who runs a café, plan for what machines could do in their work.
S4.feel: Calm, and a little envious of younger workers.
S4.quote: If a robot means some twenty-year-old never gets that click, I'm jealous and glad at the same time.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Tara is calm and future-focused, envying the young workers whose bodies robots might spare. Her best and worst cases for her crew are concrete, and she ties the outcome to what people fight for now. She still frames everything through sharing the gains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not for me but for my crew and for Owen. What would help is if the government made companies keep and retrain their workers for a set time before replacing them, and some kind of income for people in between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone asked the crews what they want from the machines. Nobody ever asks us, they ask the office. Every lad on my crew could tell you which job he'd hand to a robot tomorrow, and it's never the one the office thinks.

headlineQuote: Every lad on my crew could tell you which job he'd hand to a robot tomorrow, and it's never the one the office thinks.
portrait: Tara Zhang is a 58-year-old site supervisor for a timber-frame prefab builder who uses AI every day to translate safety talks and plan deliveries. She's comfortable with money and sees robots as a chance to make building safer, so she's actually disappointed by the plateau. In every scenario she wants the gains shared with her crew and would fight from inside the company, even leading the robot rollout to protect people. The two-year AGI picture leaves her uneasy for her crew and her son, but with more time she'd turn her last working years into a mission training robot crews. She plans to teach at the college after retiring.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because of what it would do to her crew and to her son's bank job.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making companies keep and retrain workers for a set time before replacing them, and income support for people between jobs.
